description: REQ-106's 'Lock-acquisition order (deadlock avoidance)' paragraph (behavioral-spec.md:793-802) claims resolveLoanLockAcquisitionOrder's lexicographic total-ordering is needed because, without it, 'two concurrent attempts ... might involve the same lender+borrower pair in different roles' could deadlock -- stating verbatim: 'this is the textbook total-lock-ordering deadlock-avoidance technique: because every attempt sorts its OWN two keys the SAME deterministic way, no two concurrent attempts can ever hold one lock while waiting on the other in reverse order' (line 802). This claim is analytically false for the ACTUAL, already-reused lock.mjs mechanism this SAME document cites fresh at lines 748-757. Re-read fresh this session (lock.mjs:153-158, 187-209): acquire() is a single, non-blocking, atomic fs.open(file,'wx') attempt -- if it fails (EEXIST) it tries reclaimStaleLock ONCE (also non-blocking: fs.stat + a single fs.rename attempt) and then returns true/false; withGigLock's own docstring (lock.mjs:174-179) states explicitly: 'If another call already holds the lock, returns a fail-closed rejection WITHOUT ever calling fn() -- no queueing, no waiting, no window where two callers can both reach a network settle.' There is NO retry loop, NO blocking wait, and NO code path in which a caller holds one lock while suspended waiting for another. Classical lock-ordering deadlock (a circular hold-and-wait: party A holds resource 1 and blocks waiting for resource 2, while party B holds resource 2 and blocks waiting for resource 1) is structurally impossible against a fail-fast, non-blocking mutual-exclusion primitive, REGARDLESS of what order the two nested withGigLock calls acquire their keys in -- a caller that fails to acquire its INNER lock simply returns {ok:false} immediately and its own OUTER lock is released in withGigLock's finally block (lock.mjs:203-208), never held-and-waited. Concretely walking the design with real IDs: (1) automaton lends to Franklin (keys {loan_automaton, loan_borrower_Franklin}) concurrently with Franklin lending to automaton (keys {loan_Franklin, loan_borrower_automaton}) -- these are FOUR entirely distinct strings; the two attempts share ZERO lock keys and can never interact, ordered or not. (2) automaton and Franklin both lend to the SAME new borrower X (the actual PROP-106n scenario, keys {loan_automaton, loan_borrower_X} vs {loan_Franklin, loan_borrower_X}) -- the ONLY shared key across the two attempts is loan_borrower_X; deadlock fundamentally requires at least TWO resources shared between two parties in reversed acquisition order, and here there is never more than ONE shared key between any two concurrent issuance attempts (the lender-key namespace loan_<lenderId> and borrower-key namespace loan_borrower_<borrowerId> are disjoint by the very naming convention REQ-106 itself documents at lines 808-815). So neither precondition for real lock-ordering deadlock (>=2 shared resources acquired in reversed order, AND blocking waits) is ever present in this design -- the ordering mechanism is solving a problem that cannot occur, for two independent reasons, not one. PROP-106m (verification-architecture.md, the row documenting resolveLoanLockAcquisitionOrder) and its Tier-1 unit test only assert that the sort function returns a correctly-ordered pair -- it does not and cannot exercise an actual deadlock, because none is constructible against this mechanism; no Tier-2 test anywhere in the 149-line proof-obligation table attempts to induce or measure a hang/deadlock (PROP-106n tests the REAL property that matters here -- exactly one of two cross-lender attempts on the same borrower succeeds -- a correctness property, not a deadlock-avoidance property). This means the spec's own stated JUSTIFICATION for a piece of its concurrency design is unsound, even though the mechanism itself remains harmless. This matters for verification readiness because: (a) a future maintainer reading this rationale could reasonably conclude that REMOVING the total-lock-ordering rule (e.g. reverting to 'always acquire the lender lock first, then the borrower lock', a simpler and equally correct rule given the disjoint namespaces) would reintroduce a deadlock risk -- it would not, since none exists either way; (b) if lock.mjs is ever refactored to add retry-with-backoff semantics (making acquire() genuinely blocking), the CURRENT total-ordering rule would suddenly become load-bearing for a real reason the spec's own analysis never correctly identified, and nobody maintaining this code would understand why; (c) five consecutive spec-review iterations (including iteration 5's own detailed FIND-401 fix, which re-read lock.mjs's exact line numbers for OTHER purposes) accepted this plausible-sounding but incorrect concurrency-theory claim without catching it, which is itself a signal that convergence review is starting to rubber-stamp confident-sounding prose rather than re-deriving it.

evidence.snippet: Lock-acquisition order (deadlock avoidance): ... THE SYSTEM SHALL acquire, as the OUTER lock, whichever of the two lock-key STRINGS sorts lexicographically FIRST ... This is the textbook total-lock-ordering deadlock-avoidance technique: because every attempt sorts its OWN two keys the SAME deterministic way, no two concurrent attempts can ever hold one lock while waiting on the other in reverse order.

crossCheck.note: acquire() (lines 153-158) is a single non-blocking attempt (tryCreateLockFile, then at most one reclaimStaleLock attempt); withGigLock's own docstring (lines 174-179) states a caller that cannot acquire the lock is rejected immediately, 'no queueing, no waiting'; withGigLock's implementation (lines 187-209) has no retry loop -- a failed acquire returns {ok:false} in a single pass. This directly contradicts the 'hold one lock while waiting on the other' scenario the spec's own deadlock-avoidance rationale (behavioral-spec.md:802) depends on for its justification. verification-architecture.md's PROP-106m (the proof obligation for resolveLoanLockAcquisitionOrder) tests only that the sort function returns the correct [outerKey, innerKey] pair -- it asserts nothing about deadlock, and no Tier-2 test in the document attempts to construct or measure one.
